source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's NVA5-NVA7 campus in Sterling, Virginia publishes 116 MW of IT capacity, the third largest figure of any mapped Virginia facility and about 4.5 percent of the state's 2,563.4 MW of published capacity.

The more telling number is the gap around it. Virginia has 376 mapped data centers but only 29 that publish a megawatt figure. Most of the state's footprint is invisible at the level that matters for AI, and this campus is one of the few that is not. Published capacity is a minority practice, so any statewide total built from it undercounts what is actually there.

The 116 MW is capacity, not consumption. CyrusOne publishes no rack count, no accelerator count, and no power usage effectiveness on the spec page read here. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 116 MW is roughly 2,900 racks. At 10 kW per rack, typical of older enterprise colocation, it is roughly 11,600. Neither is the operator's claim, and the split between AI training and traditional colocation at this site is not published. What the figure does establish is that the campus is sized for a meaningful share of a regional grid's load, and that electrical capacity, not building shell, is the number that matters.

The certifications field is empty, which limits what can be said rather than proving nothing exists. The address and postal code are unpublished, so the campus can be placed in Sterling and no more precisely. The judgment that this campus matters to AI rests on the 116 MW and its rank, both published, and on the rack-level composition, which is not.
